items.title: Composition & Vertical Structure of the Atmosphere
items.body:
### Composition & Vertical Structure of the Atmosphere

**In one line**
The atmosphere is the envelope of gases around the Earth; it is a fixed **mix of gases** and is stacked in **five layers**, of which the bottom one holds all our weather.

**Why it is asked**
Prelims asks the two main gases and their percentages, which layer has the weather, which holds the ozone layer, and which reflects radio waves.

**The story**
Dry air is mostly **nitrogen (~78%)**, which is inert and simply dilutes the oxygen, and **oxygen (~21%)**, which we breathe and which supports burning. The small remainder is **argon (0.93%)**, **carbon dioxide (0.03%)** and traces. On top of this sit two hugely important variables: **water vapour** (0–5% by volume, most near the equator, least at the poles), the source of every cloud, fog and raindrop; and tiny **dust and salt particles** that scatter sunlight (giving the blue sky and red sunsets) and act as the nuclei on which water condenses. Going up, the air is organised into layers by how its **temperature changes with height**: the **troposphere** (all weather), the **stratosphere** (ozone layer, calm — ideal for jet flight), the **mesosphere** (meteors burn up, coldest top), the **thermosphere** (contains the ionosphere that bounces radio waves, and the ISS orbits here), and the wispy **exosphere** where light gases leak into space.

**Why it matters**
The ozone layer in the stratosphere shields life from ultraviolet rays, and CO₂ and water vapour trap heat — so composition and structure directly set up the greenhouse effect and climate.

**Picture it**

| Layer (bottom → top) | Extent | Key feature |
|---|---|---|
| Troposphere | ~13 km (16 equator, 6 poles) | all weather; lapse rate 6.5°C per 1000 m; ends at tropopause |
| Stratosphere | up to ~50 km | ozone layer (15–30 km); stable, good for flying |
| Mesosphere | 50–80 km | meteors burn up; coldest at the mesopause (~−80°C) |
| Thermosphere | above 80 km | temperature rises fast; ionosphere reflects radio waves |
| Exosphere | outermost | very thin; hydrogen and helium escape to space |

**Terms explained**
- **Lapse rate** — the rate at which temperature falls as you go up (normally 6.5°C per 1000 m).
- **Ozone layer** — a band of ozone gas in the stratosphere that absorbs harmful ultraviolet radiation.
- **Ionosphere** — the electrically charged part of the thermosphere that reflects radio waves back to Earth.

**Don't confuse**
- **Troposphere vs stratosphere**: weather is in the troposphere; the ozone layer is in the stratosphere.
- **Mesosphere vs thermosphere**: meteors burn in the mesosphere; radio waves bounce off the thermosphere's ionosphere.
- **Ozone 'layer' vs ozone 'hole'**: the layer protects us; the hole is its thinning over Antarctica.

**Which gas does what with radiation**
Carbon dioxide absorbs terrestrial long-wave radiation and re-radiates it, warming the lower atmosphere. Ozone in the stratosphere absorbs most incoming ultraviolet radiation. Water vapour is transparent to incoming short-wave solar radiation but absorbs outgoing long-wave radiation. Nitrogen, by contrast, is inert — it is not the gas that drives atmospheric chemistry.

**Don't confuse — ozone vs global warming**
The ozone layer in the stratosphere shields life from ultraviolet rays; it is **not** the principal gas responsible for recent global warming. Recent warming is driven mainly by **carbon dioxide, methane and nitrous oxide**, released above all by **burning fossil fuels** (coal, oil, gas). The **IPCC (Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change)** is the UN body that assesses this climate science.

**Remember it**
Layers upward spell **'The Sun My Turtle Eats'** = Troposphere, Stratosphere, Mesosphere, Thermosphere, Exosphere.

**TL;DR**
- Dry air ≈ 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen, 0.93% argon, 0.03% CO₂.
- Water vapour (0–5%) is the source of clouds, fog, dew and rain, and a greenhouse regulator.
- Troposphere holds all weather; normal lapse rate is 6.5°C per 1000 m.
- Ozone layer sits in the stratosphere (15–30 km) and absorbs UV radiation.
- The ionosphere (in the thermosphere) reflects radio waves; meteors burn in the mesosphere.

items.title: Insolation, Heat Budget & Temperature
items.body:
### Insolation, Heat Budget & Temperature

**In one line**
**Insolation** is the sunlight the Earth receives, and the **heat budget** is the book-keeping that shows the Earth sends back exactly as much energy as it takes in — so its average temperature stays steady.

**Why it is asked**
Prelims asks the budget figures (35 reflected, 51 absorbed by the surface), the meaning of albedo, and the conditions that cause a temperature inversion.

**The story**
**Insolation** (incoming solar radiation) is strongest in the tropics and weakest at the poles. Part of it is simply bounced straight back — the **albedo**. Think of 100 units arriving at the top of the atmosphere: about **35 units are reflected** back to space (27 off cloud tops, 2 off ice/snow, 6 scattered), and the other **65 units are absorbed** (14 by the atmosphere, 51 by the surface). The warmed surface then re-radiates its 51 units as **long-wave (terrestrial) radiation** — 17 straight to space and 34 into the atmosphere. The atmosphere, holding 14 (direct) + 34 (from the surface) = 48 units, radiates them out too. So the outgoing **17 + 48 = 65 units** exactly matches the incoming 65, and the Earth neither heats up nor cools down overall. A key twist: the Earth is heated **from below** — the ground warms first and then warms the air above it.

**Why it matters**
This balance is what the enhanced greenhouse effect disturbs; understanding the baseline budget is the key to understanding global warming.

**Picture it**

```
IN 100 units
 ├─ 35 reflected (albedo): 27 clouds + 2 ice/snow + 6 scatter
 └─ 65 absorbed: 14 atmosphere + 51 surface
OUT 65 units
 ├─ 17 surface → space (direct long-wave)
 └─ 48 atmosphere → space (14 direct + 34 from surface)
IN 65 = OUT 65  → steady temperature
```

**Terms explained**
- **Albedo** — the fraction of incoming radiation a surface reflects (fresh snow and cloud tops are high-albedo).
- **Terrestrial radiation** — the long-wave heat the Earth's surface sends back out after being warmed.
- **Temperature inversion** — the normal fall of temperature with height is reversed, so warm air sits over cold.
- **Isotherm** — a line on a map joining places with the same temperature.

**Don't confuse**
- **Insolation vs albedo**: insolation is energy received; albedo is the share reflected away.
- **Short-wave vs long-wave**: incoming sunlight is short-wave; the Earth re-radiates long-wave heat (which greenhouse gases absorb).
- **Normal lapse vs inversion**: normally it gets colder with height; in an inversion it gets warmer with height.

**Remember it**
An inversion needs a **long, clear, calm winter night** — the ground radiates heat away fast and chills the air just above it, trapping fog and smoke.

**TL;DR**
- Of incoming insolation, ~35 units are reflected (albedo) and 65 absorbed (14 atmosphere + 51 surface).
- The heat budget balances: 65 in = 65 out, keeping global temperature steady.
- Earth is heated from below by long-wave terrestrial radiation absorbed by CO₂/water vapour.
- Temperature controls: latitude, altitude, distance from sea, air masses and ocean currents.
- Temperature inversion (warm over cold) forms on clear, calm winter nights and traps fog/pollutants; high thin clouds warm the surface while low thick clouds cool it.

items.title: Pressure Belts & Planetary/Local Winds
items.body:
### Pressure Belts & Planetary/Local Winds

**In one line**
Uneven heating of the Earth creates belts of high and low air pressure, and air flowing from high to low pressure — bent by the Earth's spin — gives us the world's **winds**.

**Why it is asked**
Prelims asks the four pressure belts and their nicknames, which are thermal vs dynamic, the Coriolis rule, and where famous local winds (Loo, Chinook, Mistral) blow.

**The story**
There are **four pressure belts** from the equator to each pole. At the equator the air is heated, rises and leaves a calm **equatorial low (the doldrums / ITCZ)**. The risen air sinks around 30° to form the **subtropical high (the Horse latitudes)**. Where cold polar air meets warm tropical air near 60° there is a stormy **subpolar low**, and over the frozen poles the cold, dense air makes a **polar high**. The equatorial low and polar high are **thermal** (caused by heating/cooling); the subtropical high and subpolar low are **dynamic** (caused by air movement). These belts **slide north in June and south in December**, following the overhead Sun — the basis of monsoons. Air blowing between the belts gives the **planetary winds**: **trade winds** (from 30° toward the equator), **westerlies** (30° toward 60°) and **polar easterlies** (poles toward 60°). The spinning Earth adds the **Coriolis force**, which bends winds to the **right in the Northern Hemisphere and left in the Southern**, zero at the equator and strongest at the poles. In the Southern Hemisphere there is little land between 40°S and 60°S to obstruct them, so over this open ocean the westerlies rage unobstructed as the **Roaring Forties, Furious Fifties and Screaming Sixties**.

**Why it matters**
The wind belts move the pressure systems, jet streams and monsoons that decide where and when it rains.

**Picture it**

| Belt | Latitude | Nature |
|---|---|---|
| Equatorial low (ITCZ / doldrums) | 0° | thermal; calm, rising air |
| Subtropical high (Horse latitudes) | ~30°N/S | dynamic; descending air |
| Subpolar low | ~60°N/S | dynamic; cyclonic storms |
| Polar high | 90°N/S | thermal; cold dense air |

**Famous local winds — where they blow**

| Wind | Character | Region |
|---|---|---|
| Loo | hot, dry (May–June) | northern plains of India |
| Chinook | warm, dry 'snow-eater' | eastern slopes of the Rockies |
| Foehn | warm, dry | leeward slopes of the Alps |
| Mistral | cold | Rhone valley, France |
| Sirocco | hot, dry, dusty | blows from the Sahara towards the Mediterranean |
| Harmattan | hot, dry, dusty north-easterly, nicknamed 'the Doctor' | West Africa |
| Santa Ana | hot, dry offshore wind | southern California |
| Berg | hot, dry wind descending to the coast | South Africa |

**Terms explained**
- **ITCZ (Inter-Tropical Convergence Zone)** — the equatorial low belt where the two trade winds meet; also called the monsoon trough over India.
- **Coriolis force** — the apparent sideways push on moving air caused by the Earth's rotation.
- **Local wind** — a wind peculiar to one region, often named locally (Loo, Chinook).

**Don't confuse**
- **Thermal vs dynamic belts**: equatorial low and polar high are thermal; subtropical high and subpolar low are dynamic.
- **Warm vs cold local winds**: Loo (N. India, hot), Chinook/Foehn (warm, 'snow-eaters'); Mistral (France, cold), Sirocco (hot, dusty).
- **Coriolis direction**: right in the north, left in the south — never the reverse.

**Remember it**
Warm descending winds warm the leeward side: **Foehn (Alps) and Chinook (Rockies)** both melt snow.

**TL;DR**
- Four pressure belts: equatorial low, subtropical high (Horse latitudes), subpolar low, polar high.
- Equatorial low and polar high are thermal; subtropical high and subpolar low are dynamic.
- Planetary winds: trade winds, westerlies, polar easterlies, controlled by the pressure belts.
- SH westerlies = Roaring Forties / Furious Fifties / Screaming Sixties because of open ocean.
- Loo (N. India hot), Chinook (Rockies warm), Mistral (France cold), Foehn (leeward Alps warm).

items.title: Cyclones — Tropical vs Temperate, Naming & AP Coast
items.body:
### Cyclones — Tropical vs Temperate, Naming & AP Coast

**In one line**
A cyclone is a spinning storm around a centre of low pressure; the violent warm-sea **tropical** kind and the frontal mid-latitude **temperate** kind are opposites in almost every way.

**Why it is asked**
Prelims asks the conditions for cyclone birth, the eye/eye-wall structure, the tropical-vs-temperate contrasts, who names Indian Ocean cyclones, and AP coast case studies (Hudhud).

**The story**
A **tropical cyclone** is born over a **warm sea (surface temperature above 27°C)** that supplies heat and moisture. It also needs the **Coriolis force** to make it spin (so none form within about 5° of the equator), **low vertical wind shear**, a pre-existing low and upper-air divergence to pull air out of the top. Its structure is a calm, clear **eye** in the centre, a surrounding **eye wall** of the fiercest winds and rain, and outer spiralling **rain bands**. It dies quickly after **landfall** because its moisture supply is cut off. The same storm has different names: **Cyclone** (Indian Ocean), **Hurricane** (Atlantic), **Typhoon** (W. Pacific), **Willy-willy** (W. Australia). A **temperate (extratropical) cyclone** is quite different — it forms along the **polar front** where cold and warm air meet, has clear **fronts**, moves **west to east**, and can form over land or sea; tropical cyclones instead move **east to west**, form only over sea, and are more destructive.

**Why it matters**
Andhra Pradesh's long east coast is one of India's most cyclone-battered, so this topic is both a Prelims and a Mains disaster-management staple.

**Picture it**

| Feature | Tropical cyclone | Temperate cyclone |
|---|---|---|
| Forms over | warm sea only (SST > 27°C) | land or sea, along the polar front |
| Fronts | none | clear warm and cold fronts |
| Moves | east → west | west → east |
| Season (India) | Oct–Nov (and pre-monsoon) | winter (western disturbances) |

**Terms explained**
- **Eye / eye wall** — the calm low-pressure centre, ringed by the eye wall of the strongest winds.
- **RSMC** — Regional Specialised Meteorological Centre; IMD New Delhi is one of six worldwide and names north-Indian-Ocean cyclones.
- **Landfall** — the moment a cyclone's centre crosses the coast.

**Don't confuse**
- **Tropical vs temperate movement**: tropical go east→west; temperate go west→east.
- **Cyclone vs hurricane vs typhoon**: same storm, different ocean (Indian / Atlantic / W. Pacific).
- **Bay of Bengal vs Arabian Sea**: the Bay is far more cyclone-prone, so AP's east coast is hit more often.

**Remember it**
AP's cyclone peak is the **post-monsoon Oct–Nov** season; **Hudhud (2014)** hitting Visakhapatnam is the model case study.

**Naming & the AP coast**
The **IMD** names north-Indian-Ocean cyclones under the **WMO/ESCAP** panel (8 members from 2000, +5 in 2018 = 13). The **Bay of Bengal** is far more cyclogenic than the Arabian Sea, so the **AP east coast (~974 km)** is highly exposed, peaking in **Oct–Nov**. **Cyclone Hudhud (Oct 2014)** devastated Visakhapatnam.

**Cyclones that struck the Andhra Pradesh coast**

| Cyclone | When | Landfall | IMD category / impact | Name given by |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Hudhud | 12 October 2014 | Visakhapatnam | Extremely Severe Cyclonic Storm; its remnants caused a deadly snowstorm disaster in Nepal | Oman |
| Titli | October 2018 | northern Andhra Pradesh (Srikakulam belt) | Very Severe Cyclonic Storm | Pakistan |
| Michaung | December 2023 | near Bapatla, after flooding Chennai | Severe Cyclonic Storm | Myanmar |
| Montha | late October 2025 (night of 28 October) | near Narasapuram | Severe Cyclonic Storm; damaged crops over tens of thousands of hectares (about 87,000 ha), so the state sought central relief | Thailand |

The IMD, as the RSMC New Delhi, also issues cyclone advisories to the other countries in the region.

**TL;DR**
- Tropical cyclones need SST > 27°C and the Coriolis force; none form within ~5° of the equator.
- Structure: calm eye, violent eye wall, spiralling rain bands; they weaken after landfall.
- Tropical cyclones move E→W (sea only); temperate cyclones move W→E along the polar front with fronts.
- IMD (an RSMC) names north-Indian-Ocean cyclones under WMO/ESCAP (13 member nations).
- Bay of Bengal > Arabian Sea in cyclones; AP east coast peak season is Oct–Nov; Hudhud (2014) hit Visakhapatnam.

items.title: Indian Monsoon Mechanism, ENSO & IOD
items.body:
### Indian Monsoon Mechanism, ENSO & IOD

**In one line**
The monsoon is a **seasonal reversal of winds** that brings India its rain, and its strength each year is nudged by two ocean see-saws — **ENSO** in the Pacific and the **IOD** in the Indian Ocean.

**Why it is asked**
Prelims asks the driving mechanism (land–sea heating, ITCZ shift), the SW-vs-NE monsoon contrast (crucial for AP), and how El Niño, La Niña and the IOD affect rainfall.

**The story**
Land heats and cools faster than the sea. In summer the land of north-west India becomes very hot, the air rises and leaves a **thermal low**; the **ITCZ (monsoon trough)** shifts north, and moist air is pulled all the way from the southern Indian Ocean. Crossing the equator it is bent by the Coriolis force and arrives as the **south-west (summer) monsoon**, onsetting over **Kerala around 1 June**. It is helped along by the **cross-equatorial Somali jet**, the **tropical easterly jet**, and the shifting of the subtropical westerly jet to north of the Himalayas. In winter the pattern reverses: the land cools, winds blow offshore, and the **north-east (retreating) monsoon** of Oct–Dec picks up moisture over the Bay of Bengal and rains on **coastal Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu**. A sudden heavy start is a **'burst'**; a dry spell within the season is a **'break'**. Two ocean patterns tune the strength: **El Niño** (a warm central-east Pacific) usually gives a **weaker** monsoon, **La Niña** conditions a **good** (often above-normal) one (together with the Southern Oscillation this is **ENSO**); and a **positive Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD)** — a warm western Indian Ocean — usually **helps** rainfall and can cancel out an El Niño.

**Why it matters**
The monsoon is the lifeline of Indian and AP agriculture; a weak year means drought, an excess year means floods.

**Picture it**

| Feature | South-west (summer) | North-east (retreating) |
|---|---|---|
| Period | June–September | October–December |
| Onset | Kerala ~1 June | after SW withdrawal |
| Main rain area | most of India | coastal AP & Tamil Nadu |

**Jet streams and the monsoon**
Jet streams are fast, narrow bands of geostrophic westerly winds in the upper troposphere. In winter the **subtropical westerly jet** blows south of the Himalayas and steers the **western disturbances** that bring winter rain to north-west India. In summer it shifts **north of the Himalayas** — this northward shift signals the **onset of the monsoon** — and the **Tropical Easterly Jet** develops over the Indian subcontinent and aids the south-west monsoon.

**Terms explained**
- **ITCZ / monsoon trough** — the equatorial low belt whose northward shift drags in the summer monsoon.
- **ENSO** — El Niño–Southern Oscillation, the Pacific warm/cool see-saw that modulates the monsoon.
- **IOD** — the sea-temperature difference between the western and the south-eastern (near Indonesia) tropical Indian Ocean.

**Don't confuse**
- **SW vs NE monsoon**: SW (Jun–Sep) waters most of India; NE (Oct–Dec) is the one that rains on coastal AP/TN.
- **El Niño vs La Niña**: El Niño weakens the monsoon; La Niña strengthens it.
- **IOD vs ENSO**: IOD is the Indian Ocean's see-saw (western vs eastern Indian Ocean) — not the Pacific; a positive IOD can offset an El Niño.

**IOD in one line** — the Indian Ocean Dipole is the sea-surface-temperature difference between the western and the eastern tropical **Indian** Ocean (not the Pacific); an IOD event can influence — even offset — the impact of El Niño on the Indian monsoon.

**Remember it**
**SW = 'Summer, Wet, whole country'; NE = 'Now East coast (AP/TN) in winter'.**

**TL;DR**
- The monsoon is a seasonal wind reversal driven by land–sea heating and the seasonal shift of the ITCZ.
- SW monsoon: June–Sept, onsets over Kerala ~1 June, waters most of India; aided by the Somali & easterly jets.
- NE (retreating) monsoon: Oct–Dec, brings most rain to coastal AP and Tamil Nadu.
- 'Burst' = sudden monsoon onset; 'break' = a dry spell within the season.
- El Niño weakens and La Niña strengthens the monsoon; a positive IOD favours rainfall and can offset an El Niño.

items.title: Condensation, Precipitation & Köppen Classification
items.body:
### Condensation, Precipitation & Köppen Classification

**In one line**
When moist air cools, its vapour **condenses** into dew, fog, clouds and finally **rain**, and **Köppen's scheme** is the standard way of labelling the world's climates from the vegetation they support.

**Why it is asked**
Prelims asks the dew/frost/smog conditions, the three ways rain is produced (convectional, orographic, cyclonic), and the Köppen letter codes (Af, Am, BWh, Cs) and India's type.

**The story**
Warm air can hold more water vapour than cold air. **Relative humidity** tells us how full the air is (actual vapour as a percentage of what it could hold at that temperature). When air is cooled to its **dew point** it becomes saturated and vapour starts to condense. If the dew point is **above 0°C** you get **dew**; if it is **at or below 0°C** you get **frost**; cooling in the free air gives **fog, mist and clouds**, and fog mixed with smoke is **smog**. For rain, moist air must be lifted and cooled, and there are three ways this happens: **convectional** (the ground heats the air which rises — typical equatorial afternoons), **orographic** (air is forced up a mountain, raining on the windward side and leaving a dry **rain shadow** to leeward — the Western Ghats), and **cyclonic/frontal** (warm air rides over cold along a front, as in temperate cyclones). **Köppen (1918)** then grouped the world's climates by linking them to vegetation, using letters: **A** tropical, **B** dry, **C** warm temperate, **D** cold snow-forest, **E** polar, plus **H** highland.

**Why it matters**
These ideas explain India's rainfall pattern (orographic Western Ghats, convectional afternoons) and let you label AP's climate (mostly Aw/Am) in one code.

**Picture it**

| Rain type | Cause | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Convectional | surface heating lifts warm air | equatorial afternoons |
| Orographic | air forced up a mountain; rain shadow to leeward | Western Ghats |
| Cyclonic / frontal | warm air lifted over cold along a front | temperate cyclones |

**Four cloud types to recognise**

| Cloud | Height | Looks like / brings |
|---|---|---|
| Cirrus | high (6–12 km) | high, thin, wispy ice-crystal clouds ('mare's tails') |
| Cumulus | vertical, low base | heaped fair-weather clouds with a flat base and cauliflower top |
| Nimbostratus | low | low, thick grey layer giving continuous steady rain or snow |
| Cumulonimbus | towering, low base to high top | thunderstorm cloud producing heavy rain, hail and lightning |

**Terms explained**
- **Relative humidity** — how full of vapour the air is, as a percentage of its capacity at that temperature.
- **Dew point** — the temperature at which air becomes saturated and condensation begins.
- **Rain shadow** — the dry leeward side of a mountain where descending air gives little rain.
- **Köppen groups** — A tropical, B dry, C warm temperate, D cold snow-forest, E polar, H highland.

**The four Köppen codes the exam asks most**

| Code | Climate | What it means |
|---|---|---|
| Af | Tropical wet (rainforest) | rain throughout the year, no dry month |
| Am | Tropical monsoon | heavy summer rain, a short dry winter |
| BWh | Hot subtropical desert | dry (B), desert (W), hot (h) |
| Cs | Mediterranean | dry summer (s), wet winter |

**Don't confuse**
- **Dew vs frost**: dew needs a dew point above 0°C; frost needs it at or below 0°C.
- **Orographic rain side**: it falls on the **windward** side; the **leeward** side is the dry rain shadow.
- **Köppen temperature vs rain groups**: four groups are temperature-based; **group B (dry) is precipitation-based**.

**Remember it**
Most of India is **Am/Aw** (tropical monsoon / wet-and-dry), with **Cwa** over the north plains and **BW/BS** in the north-west desert.

**TL;DR**
- Dew forms with a dew point above 0°C; frost at or below 0°C; fog + smoke = smog.
- Precipitation types: convectional (heating), orographic (mountains), cyclonic/frontal (converging air).
- Köppen (1918) links climate to vegetation; groups A, B, C, D, E and highland H.
- Four Köppen groups are temperature-based; group B is precipitation-based.
- Af = tropical wet, Am = tropical monsoon, BWh = hot desert, Cs = Mediterranean; India is mainly Am/Aw.

items.body:
### Air Masses & Fronts

**In one line**
An **air mass** is a huge block of air with one temperature and humidity throughout, and a **front** is the sloping battle-line where two different air masses meet — the birthplace of temperate-cyclone weather.

**Why it is asked**
Prelims asks the air-mass codes (cP, mT, cT, mP), the weather of cold vs warm fronts, and what an occluded front means in a cyclone's life.

**The story**
If air sits for days over a large, calm, uniform area — a **source region** such as a warm ocean, a snowfield or a desert — it takes on that region's temperature and humidity and becomes an **air mass**. We label it with two letters: the first for moisture (**c** = continental/dry, **m** = maritime/moist), the second for temperature (**P/A** = polar/arctic cold, **T** = tropical hot). So **cP** is cold-dry Siberian air, **mT** warm-moist tropical-ocean air, **cT** hot-dry desert air and **mP** cold-moist high-latitude-ocean air. As an air mass travels it is **modified** — cold air crossing a warm sea gains heat and moisture and turns unstable. When two contrasting air masses meet along the **polar front**, the lighter warm air is forced up over the denser cold air, forming a **front**. A **cold front** is steep: cold air shoves under the warm air sharply, giving towering cumulonimbus, brief violent squally rain, then a sharp temperature drop and clearing. A **warm front** is gentle: warm air glides slowly up, giving an orderly cloud sequence (cirrus → cirrostratus → altostratus → nimbostratus) and prolonged steady rain, then warming. A faster cold front can catch up and lift the warm air clear of the ground — an **occluded front**, which marks the dying stage of a mid-latitude cyclone. A **stationary front** is where neither air mass can push the other.

**Why it matters**
Fronts are the engine of temperate-cyclone weather and winter 'western disturbances', which Prelims links to north-west Indian rainfall.

**Picture it**

| Front | Slope | Weather |
|---|---|---|
| Cold | steep | cumulonimbus, brief heavy squally rain, then temperature drop and clearing |
| Warm | gentle | cirrus→nimbostratus cloud sequence, prolonged steady rain, then warming |
| Occluded | complex | warm air lifted aloft; the dying stage of a cyclone |
| Stationary | — | neither air mass advances; persistent dull, cloudy weather |

**The four air masses and their source regions**

| Code | Name | Source region | Character |
|---|---|---|---|
| cP | Continental Polar | Siberia / northern Canada in winter | cold and dry |
| mT | Maritime Tropical | warm tropical oceans | warm and humid |
| cT | Continental Tropical | the Sahara and other desert interiors | hot and dry |
| mP | Maritime Polar | cold high-latitude oceans (North Atlantic/Pacific) | cold and moist |

**Two kinds of occlusion**
An occluded front forms when a faster-moving cold front overtakes the warm front ahead, lifting the entire warm sector off the ground. In a **cold occlusion** the air behind the cold front is colder than the air ahead, so it undercuts both; in a **warm occlusion** the air behind the front is milder than the cold air ahead, so it rides up over it. Either way, occlusion is the final, dissipating stage of a mid-latitude (temperate) cyclone.

**Terms explained**
- **Source region** — a large, calm, uniform area where an air mass gets its character.
- **Front** — the sloping boundary between two air masses of different temperature/humidity.
- **Occlusion** — when a cold front overtakes a warm front and lifts the warm sector off the ground.

**Don't confuse**
- **Cold vs warm front**: cold = steep, brief violent storms; warm = gentle, long steady rain.
- **First vs second letter in codes**: first = moisture (c dry / m moist); second = temperature (P/A cold / T hot).
- **Occluded vs stationary**: occluded = fronts merge (cyclone dying); stationary = fronts stuck, neither moves.

**Remember it**
In the codes, the **first letter = moisture** (c dry, m moist) and the **second = temperature** (P/A cold, T hot).

**TL;DR**
- Air mass = a large body of air with uniform temperature/humidity from a uniform source region.
- Classification: cP/cA cold-dry, mP cold-moist, cT hot-dry, mT warm-moist; air masses are modified along their track.
- Cold front: steep slope, cumulonimbus, brief violent rain, then temperature falls.
- Warm front: gentle slope, cirrus→nimbostratus, prolonged steady rain, then warming.
- Occluded front = cold front overtakes warm front (the dissipating stage of a temperate cyclone); a stationary front barely moves.
keyPoints: Air mass = large body of air with uniform temperature/humidity from a uniform source region.
Classification: cP/cA cold-dry, mP cold-moist, cT hot-dry, mT warm-moist.
Air masses are modified along their track (cold air over warm sea becomes warm, moist, unstable).
Cold front: steep slope, cumulonimbus, brief violent rain, then temperature falls.
Warm front: gentle slope, cloud sequence cirrus→nimbostratus, prolonged steady rain, then warming.
Occluded front forms when a cold front overtakes a warm front — the dissipating stage of a temperate cyclone.
Stationary front: neither air mass can displace the other.

items.title: Atmosphere — Full Gas Table, Particles & Layer Details
items.body:
### The atmosphere in detail

**In one line**
The atmosphere is a mechanical mixture of gases, water vapour and particles held by gravity, layered from the weather-making **troposphere** up to the nebula-thin **exosphere**.

**The story**
The atmosphere is held to the Earth by **gravity**; our source gives its height as about **16,000–29,000 km**. Without it the Earth would be barren like the Moon.

| Gas | % by volume | Role |
|---|---|---|
| Nitrogen | 78 | a **diluent**, chemically inactive |
| Oxygen | 21 | breathing and **combustion** |
| Argon | 0.93 | the third gas |
| Carbon dioxide | 0.03 (today about 0.04) | photosynthesis; **greenhouse gas** that absorbs and re-radiates terrestrial heat |
| Neon | 0.0018 | |
| Helium | 0.0005 | |
| Ozone | 0.00006 | absorbs most **ultraviolet** rays |
| Hydrogen | 0.00005 | |
| Krypton, xenon, methane | traces | |

Besides CO₂, **methane**, **nitrous oxide** and water vapour are greenhouse gases.

**Water vapour** is **0–5%** by volume; it **decreases from the equator to the poles** with falling temperature. It is almost transparent to incoming **short-wave** radiation but absorbs outgoing **long-wave** radiation, so it warms the lower air.

**Particulate matter** (dust, salt, pollen, smoke, soot, volcanic ash) **scatters** sunlight — giving red and orange skies at sunrise and sunset; **selective scattering** gives the **blue** sky. **Salt particles** act as **hygroscopic nuclei** on which water drops form.

**Layer details**

| Layer | Details |
|---|---|
| Troposphere | "zone of **mixing**"; source average height **13 km** (16 km at the equator, 6 km at the poles; NCERT gives ~18 km and ~8 km); **higher in summer**, lower in winter; top = **tropopause** (about **1.5 km** thick, "where mixing stops") |
| Stratosphere | up to **50 km**; **ozone** layer (**ozonosphere**) at **15–30 km**; temperature **rises** with height because ozone absorbs UV; almost cloud-free, ideal for **aeroplanes**; top = stratopause |
| Mesosphere | **50–80 km**; temperature falls again to about **−80°C** at the **mesopause** (coldest); **meteors burn** up here |
| Thermosphere | temperature rises very fast; the **International Space Station** orbits here; contains the **ionosphere** (**80–400 km**), with **D, E, F and G** layers that **reflect radio waves**; auroras glow here |
| Exosphere | outermost; very thin, nebula-like air; **hydrogen and helium** escape to space |

**Lapse rate** — temperature falls about **6.5°C per 1,000 m** in the troposphere (some books give 6.4°C/km).

**Don't confuse**
Ozone is in the stratosphere, not the troposphere. Meteors burn in the mesosphere; radio waves bounce off the ionosphere (thermosphere).

**TL;DR**
- N₂ 78, O₂ 21, Ar 0.93, CO₂ 0.03(–0.04), Ne 0.0018, He 0.0005, O₃ 0.00006, H₂ 0.00005.
- Water vapour 0–5%, falls poleward; particles scatter light (blue sky, red sunsets); salt = hygroscopic nuclei.
- Troposphere "mixing", higher in summer, tropopause 1.5 km thick; stratosphere to 50 km (ozone 15–30 km).
- Mesopause −80°C; ionosphere 80–400 km (D, E, F, G layers); ISS in the thermosphere.
keyPoints: Atmosphere height about 16,000–29,000 km (source); held by gravity.
Nitrogen is a diluent and chemically inactive; oxygen supports breathing and combustion.
Water vapour 0–5% decreases from the equator poleward; transparent to short-wave, absorbs long-wave.
Dust gives red/orange sunrises and sunsets; selective scattering gives the blue sky; salt particles are hygroscopic nuclei.
Troposphere ("zone of mixing") is higher in summer; the tropopause is about 1.5 km thick.
Stratosphere to 50 km; temperature rises with height; ideal for aeroplanes.
Mesopause about −80°C; ionosphere 80–400 km with D, E, F, G layers; ISS lies in the thermosphere.

items.title: Insolation — Zones, Controlling Factors, Heat Transfer & Heat-Budget Units
items.body:
### How the Earth is heated

**In one line**
**Insolation** (incoming solar radiation) varies with latitude, the Sun's angle, day length, atmospheric transparency, sunspots and relief; the air is then heated from below by conduction, convection, advection and long-wave terrestrial radiation.

**The story**
**Climatology** is the study of atmospheric conditions over a long period. The energy radiated by the Sun is **electromagnetic radiation**; what reaches the Earth's surface is **insolation**.

**Zones of insolation**
- **Tropical zone** (between the tropics) — Sun overhead twice a year; the most insolation, little seasonal change.
- **Middle-latitude zone** (about 23.5°–66°) — one maximum and one minimum a year; seasonality grows with latitude.
- **Polar zone** (about 60°–90°) — insolation falls to **zero** in the polar night.

**Factors controlling insolation**

| Factor | Effect |
|---|---|
| Revolution | slightly more at **perihelion (3 January)** than at **aphelion (4 July)**, but other factors mask it |
| Axial tilt (66½° to the orbit) | decides the seasons — not distance |
| **Angle of incidence** | vertical rays give more energy than oblique ones — the **most important** control, stronger than day length |
| Length of day | longer days give more; yet the poles get little despite long days (oblique rays, ice reflects) |
| Transparency of the air | some radiation is absorbed, scattered or reflected on the way |
| **Sunspots** | they follow an **11-year cycle**; more sunspots → more solar energy |
| Relief | slope, aspect and elevation create local differences |

**Maximum insolation** is received over the **subtropical deserts** (clear skies); the **equator gets less than the tropics** because of clouds; at the same latitude **continents get more than oceans**. **Isohels** join places with equal sunshine. **Albedo** is the share of radiation a surface reflects.

**How the air is heated**

| Process | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Conduction | heat passing by contact; **minor**, because **air is a poor conductor** |
| Convection | vertical rising of heated air; **confined to the troposphere** |
| **Advection** | heat carried by **horizontal** movement of air — e.g. the **Loo** and **Sirocco**; causes most day-to-day weather change in middle latitudes |
| Terrestrial radiation | the heated ground radiates **long waves** that CO₂ and other greenhouse gases absorb — so the air is heated **from below** |
| Counter-radiation | heat radiated back from the atmosphere to the ground |

**Heat budget — the unit count (insolation = 100)**
- **35** units reflected (albedo): **27** from cloud tops, **2** from snow and ice, the rest scattered to space.
- **65** absorbed: **14** by the atmosphere, **51** by the surface.
- Of the 51 the Earth radiates, **17** go straight to space and **34** are absorbed by the air — **6** directly, **9** by convection and turbulence, **19** by **latent heat of condensation**.
- The atmosphere radiates **48** (14 + 34) to space; **17 + 48 = 65** = what came in, so the Earth neither warms nor cools.

**Temperature and inversion**
Heat is molecular movement; **temperature** measures how hot something is. **Isotherms** join places of equal temperature. Annual temperature range is **greater in continental interiors** than on coasts mainly because of the **land–water heating difference** (and altitude) — UPSC 2013. In an **inversion**, temperature rises with height; it is **normal all year over polar areas**, traps smoke and fog in winter, and in hills cold air sliding downslope (**air drainage**) pools in valleys — which also **protects plants from frost** on the warmer slopes.

**Don't confuse**
Advection = horizontal; convection = vertical. Albedo = reflection; insolation = incoming.

**TL;DR**
- Angle of incidence matters more than day length; sunspot cycle 11 years; max insolation over subtropical deserts.
- Conduction minor (air poor conductor); convection only in the troposphere; advection (Loo, Sirocco) horizontal.
- Heat budget: 35 reflected (27 clouds, 2 ice), 65 absorbed (14 + 51); 17 direct + 48 from air = 65 out; 19 units via latent heat.
- Continental interiors have larger annual ranges; inversion normal over poles; air drainage.
keyPoints: Insolation = solar energy received at the surface; climatology = long-term study of atmospheric conditions.
Insolation zones: tropical, middle-latitude and polar (zero in the polar night).
Angle of incidence controls insolation more than day length.
Sunspot number follows an 11-year cycle; more sunspots → more solar energy.
Maximum insolation over subtropical deserts; equator gets less than the tropics (clouds); continents more than oceans at the same latitude.
Isohels join places of equal sunshine; isotherms join places of equal temperature.
Conduction is minor because air is a poor conductor; convection is confined to the troposphere; advection is horizontal (Loo, Sirocco).
Heat budget: 27 units reflected by clouds, 2 by snow/ice; Earth radiates 51 — 17 to space, 34 absorbed (6 + 9 + 19 latent heat); atmosphere radiates 48.
Annual range is higher in continental interiors because of land–water thermal difference (UPSC 2013).
Temperature inversion is normal over polar areas; air drainage protects plants from frost.

items.title: Pressure, Wind Forces, Circulation Cells & Planetary Winds in Detail
items.body:
### Pressure and the general circulation

**In one line**
Air pressure — about **1,013.2 mb** at sea level — falls about **1 mb every 10 m**; winds blow from high to low pressure under the pressure gradient, friction and Coriolis forces, organised into three cells per hemisphere.

**The story**
**Atmospheric pressure** is the weight of a column of air over a unit area; it is measured with a **mercury** or **aneroid barometer**. The vertical pressure gradient is far larger than the horizontal one but is balanced by gravity, so we feel no strong upward winds. **Isobars** join places of equal pressure.

**Pressure-belt details**
- **Equatorial low** — thermal; only vertical currents, no horizontal flow, hence the calm **doldrums**; trade winds converge here (**ITCZ**).
- **Subtropical high (~30°)** — air rising at the equator moves poleward, cools and sinks. In the Northern Hemisphere it survives only as ocean cells — the **Azores** (Atlantic) and **Hawaiian** (Pacific) highs. Called **Horse latitudes** because becalmed sailors threw horses overboard to lighten ships.
- **Subpolar low (~60°)** — not thermal; subtropical and polar winds converge and rise; in the south it is the continuous **sub-Antarctic low**.
- **Polar high** — cold dense air; stronger over **Antarctica** than over the Arctic Ocean.
The belts **shift with the Sun** — south in the northern winter, north in summer.

**Forces on the wind**

| Force | Key facts |
|---|---|
| Pressure gradient | strong where **isobars are close**; acts perpendicular to isobars |
| Friction | greatest at the surface, up to **1–3 km**; least over the sea |
| Coriolis | right in NH, left in SH; **proportional to latitude** (zero at the equator, maximum at poles); larger for faster winds; acts **perpendicular** to the pressure gradient |

With no Coriolis force at the equator, air flows straight into a low and **fills it** — so **tropical cyclones do not form at the equator**. Aloft (2–3 km), where friction is absent and isobars are straight, the pressure gradient and Coriolis forces balance and the wind blows **parallel to the isobars** — the **geostrophic wind**. Circulation round a low is **cyclonic**, round a high **anticyclonic**; air **converges and rises** over a low, **sinks and diverges** over a high.

**Orders of circulation** — **primary** (planetary winds and pressure belts), **secondary** (cyclones, anticyclones, monsoons), **tertiary** (local winds).

**Three cells per hemisphere**
- **Hadley cell** — air rises at the ITCZ to about **14 km**, moves poleward, sinks at 30°, returns as trade winds.
- **Ferrel cell** — middle latitudes (30°–60°); surface westerlies.
- **Polar cell** — sinking polar air flows out as **polar easterlies**; they meet the westerlies at the **polar front**, breeding cyclones.

**Planetary winds**

| Wind | Belt | Direction | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Trade winds (tropical easterlies) | 30°N–30°S, towards the equator | **NE** (north-east) in NH, **SE** (south-east) in SH | warm, moist; converge and rain at the equator |
| Westerlies | 30°–60° | **SW** in NH, **NW** in SH | rain on **west coasts**; stronger in SH — Roaring Forties, Furious Fifties, Shrieking/Screaming Sixties |
| Polar easterlies | poles → 60° | NE in NH, SE in SH | cold, dry |

**PYQ facts** — The westerlies lie between **30° and 60° in each hemisphere** (not "30°N to 60°S"), and the moist air bringing **winter rain to north-west India** (western disturbances) is part of the westerlies (UPSC 2015). In the tropics the **trade winds** make **western oceans warmer** than eastern; in temperate zones the **westerlies** make **eastern oceans warmer** (UPSC 2021). **Jet streams** occur in **both hemispheres** (UPSC 2020).

**Don't confuse**
Doldrums = equatorial calm; Horse latitudes = subtropical calm. Geostrophic wind = parallel to isobars, aloft.

**TL;DR**
- 1,013.2 mb at sea level; −1 mb per 10 m; mercury/aneroid barometer; isobars.
- Azores and Hawaiian highs; sub-Antarctic low; belts shift with the Sun.
- Coriolis ∝ latitude, ⟂ pressure gradient; no cyclones at the equator; geostrophic wind parallel to isobars.
- Hadley (to ~14 km), Ferrel, Polar cells; westerlies 30°–60° each hemisphere; jets in both hemispheres.
keyPoints: Mean sea-level pressure is 1,013.2 millibar; pressure falls about 1 mb per 10 m of height.
Pressure is measured with a mercury or aneroid barometer; isobars join places of equal pressure.
Doldrums: equatorial calm with only vertical currents; Horse latitudes: subtropical calm (Azores and Hawaiian cells).
Sub-Antarctic low: the continuous subpolar low of the Southern Hemisphere.
Friction acts up to 1–3 km and is least over the sea; Coriolis force is proportional to latitude and perpendicular to the pressure gradient.
Geostrophic wind blows parallel to isobars aloft, where pressure gradient and Coriolis forces balance.
Circulation orders: primary (planetary), secondary (cyclones, monsoons), tertiary (local winds).
Hadley cell air rises to about 14 km; Ferrel and Polar cells complete the three-cell model; polar front breeds cyclones.
Trade winds: NE in the NH, SE in the SH; westerlies: SW in the NH, NW in the SH; westerlies lie 30°–60° in each hemisphere.
UPSC 2021: trade winds make tropical western oceans warmer; westerlies make temperate eastern oceans warmer.

items.title: Local Winds of the World — Breezes, Hot & Cold Winds, Full Name List
items.body:
### Local (tertiary) winds

**In one line**
Local winds come from purely local causes — land and sea, mountain and valley, or air descending a barrier — and each famous one has a home region and a nickname.

**The story**
By **day** the land heats faster, a low forms over it and the **sea breeze** blows in; at **night** the land cools faster and the **land breeze** blows out. The system is shallow — only about **1–2 km** deep (less over lakes) — and strongest in the tropics. In mountains the sunlit slopes draw air up as the **valley breeze** by day; at night cool dense air drains down as the **mountain wind**; cold air draining off plateaus and ice fields is a **katabatic** wind. Air that rains out on the windward side and descends the lee side warms **adiabatically**, giving dry warm winds such as the Foehn and Chinook.

**Hot local winds**

| Wind | Key facts |
|---|---|
| **Loo** | hot, dry, strong; northern plains of India and Pakistan in **May–June** afternoons; blows **west to east**; **45–50°C** |
| **Foehn** | warm, dry, dusty; leeward (northern) slopes of the **Alps**; **15–20°C**; melts snow for pasture and ripens **grapes** early |
| **Chinook** | hot, dry; eastern slopes of the **Rockies**; means "**snow eater**"; helps ranchers; can raise temperature by **5°C in 20 minutes** |
| **Sirocco** | hot, dry, dusty from the **Sahara** across the Mediterranean, mostly in **spring**; carries red dust ("**blood rain**"); called **Leveche** in Spain, **Khamsin** in Egypt, **Gharbi** in the Aegean |
| **Harmattan** | dry, dusty north-easterly over **West Africa** from the Sahara; brings relief from humid heat — "**the Doctor**" |

**Cold local winds**

| Wind | Key facts |
|---|---|
| **Mistral** | very cold, dry, fast; from the **Alps** through the **Rhone valley** of France to the Mediterranean; houses shielded by hedges and tree rows |
| **Bora** | cold, dry north-easterly of the **Adriatic** coast |
| **Blizzard** | violent, snow-laden polar wind (Antarctica), up to **160 km/h** and **−70°C**; called **Buran** in Eurasia |
| Tramontana, Gregale | cold winds of the Mediterranean |

**More names (match-the-region list)**

| Wind | Region |
|---|---|
| **Elephanta** | Malabar coast, India — strong southerly/south-easterly |
| **Kali Andhi** | Indo-Gangetic plain — violent dust squalls before the monsoon |
| **Santa Ana** | southern California — hot, dry |
| **Diablo** | San Francisco Bay — hot, dry offshore |
| **Zonda** | Argentina — warm wind on the eastern slope of the Andes |
| **Pampero** | Pampas of Argentina — very strong wind |
| **Shamal** | Iraq and the Persian Gulf — summer north-westerly |
| **Simoom** | Sahara and Arabian deserts — strong, dry desert wind |
| **Etesian** | Greece and Turkey — northerly |
| **Cape Doctor** | South African coast — dry south-easterly |
| **Fremantle Doctor** | Perth — cooling afternoon sea breeze |
| **Southerly Buster** | Sydney — sudden low-pressure change |
| **Karaburan** | Central Asia — "black storm" katabatic wind |
| **Squamish** | British Columbia fjords — violent wind |
| **Nor'wester** | New Zealand's South Island (in India "Nor'westers"/**Kalbaisakhi** are pre-monsoon thunderstorms of Bengal) |

**Don't confuse**
Three "doctors": Harmattan (West Africa), Cape Doctor (South Africa), Fremantle Doctor (Perth). Chinook = Rockies; Zonda = Andes.

**TL;DR**
- Sea breeze by day, land breeze by night (1–2 km deep); valley breeze by day, mountain/katabatic wind by night.
- Loo (India, 45–50°C), Foehn (Alps, grapes), Chinook (Rockies, snow eater), Sirocco (Sahara; Leveche/Khamsin/Gharbi), Harmattan (the Doctor).
- Mistral (Rhone), Bora (Adriatic), Blizzard (160 km/h, −70°C), Buran (Eurasia).
- Elephanta (Malabar), Kali Andhi (Gangetic dust squalls), Santa Ana, Zonda, Pampero, Shamal, Simoom.
keyPoints: Sea breeze by day, land breeze by night; the system is only about 1–2 km deep.
Valley breeze by day, mountain wind by night; katabatic wind = cold air draining off plateaus and ice fields.
Loo blows west to east over the northern plains in May–June at 45–50°C.
Foehn (Alps) melts snow and ripens grapes; Chinook ("snow eater") on the eastern Rockies can raise temperature 5°C in 20 minutes.
Sirocco is called Leveche in Spain, Khamsin in Egypt and Gharbi in the Aegean; it brings "blood rain".
Harmattan is called "the Doctor"; Mistral blows through the Rhone valley; Bora on the Adriatic coast.
Blizzard: up to 160 km/h and −70°C (Antarctica); Buran in Eurasia.
Elephanta — Malabar coast; Kali Andhi — dust squalls of the Indo-Gangetic plain; Zonda — Andes, Argentina; Shamal — Persian Gulf.

items.title: Air Masses, Fronts & Cyclones — Source Regions, Life Cycle, Structure & Naming Rules
items.body:
### Air masses, fronts and cyclones in detail

**In one line**
Air masses take on the character of their **source regions**; where they meet, **fronts** form and temperate cyclones grow and die; tropical cyclones draw their energy from **latent heat** over warm seas.

**The story — air masses**
An **air mass** is a large body of air with little horizontal variation in temperature and humidity. Its five source regions are: warm tropical oceans (**mT**), subtropical hot deserts (**cT**), cold high-latitude oceans (**mP**), very cold snowy continents (**cP**) and permanent ice of the Arctic and Antarctica (**cA**, continental Arctic). The formation of a front is **frontogenesis**.

**Life of a temperate (extratropical) cyclone** — it forms on the **polar front**. The front starts **stationary**; pressure drops, warm air moves poleward and cold air equatorward, setting up an **anticlockwise** (NH) circulation with a **warm front**, a **warm sector** and a **cold front**. Clouds spread ahead of the warm front; **cumulus** clouds rise along the cold front. The **cold front moves faster**, overtakes the warm front, lifts the warm air off the ground (**occlusion**) and the cyclone **dissipates**. Temperate cyclones cover a **larger area** than tropical ones and, unlike them, have a clear **frontal system**.

**Tropical cyclone — numbers and structure**

| Point | Fact |
|---|---|
| Energy source | **latent heat of condensation** in cumulonimbus clouds around the centre; moisture from the sea — so it dies after **landfall** |
| Sea temperature | above **27°C** (often quoted as **26.5°C**) |
| Other needs | Coriolis force, **small variation in vertical wind speed** (low wind shear), a pre-existing low, upper-level divergence |
| Eye | a calm region of **subsiding air** — and **warmer**, not colder, than its surroundings; **not every** cyclone develops an eye (UPSC 2020) |
| Eye wall | strongest spiralling ascent up to the tropopause; winds up to **250 km/h**; torrential rain |
| Size | circulating core about **150–250 km**; storms over the Bay of Bengal / Arabian Sea are **600–1,200 km** across |
| Speed | moves about **300–500 km a day** |
| Track | storms crossing **20°N** usually **recurve** and are more destructive |
| Hazard | **storm surges** flood coastal lowlands |
| Where absent | **South Atlantic** and **south-east Pacific**, because sea-surface temperatures are **low** (cold currents) — UPSC 2015 |

**Names by region** — **cyclones** (Indian Ocean), **hurricanes** (Atlantic), **typhoons** (western Pacific, South China Sea), **willy-willies** (Western Australia).

**Naming rules** — cyclones are named by **six RSMCs** and the Tropical Cyclone Warning Centres. **WMO and UN-ESCAP** have named north Indian Ocean storms since **2000**, when **eight** countries started (Bangladesh, India, Maldives, Myanmar, Oman, Pakistan, Sri Lanka, Thailand); in **2018** **five** joined (**Iran, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, UAE, Yemen**) — **13** in all. **IMD** (**India Meteorological Department**), the RSMC at New Delhi, names the storms and advises **12 other nations**.

**Thunderstorms and tornadoes**
A **thunderstorm** is a well-grown **cumulonimbus** cloud with thunder and lightning, caused by intense convection on hot humid days; above the freezing level it gives **hail**, and with too little moisture it gives a **dust storm**. A **tornado** is a violent descending spiral of very low pressure from a severe thunderstorm, mostly in **middle latitudes**; over the sea it is a **waterspout**.

**Don't confuse**
cP (continental polar) vs cA (continental Arctic). The eye is warm and calm; the eye wall is where the fury is.

**TL;DR**
- Air masses: mT, cT, mP, cP, cA; frontogenesis = front formation.
- Temperate cyclone: polar front → warm sector → cold front overtakes → occlusion → dies; larger than tropical cyclones.
- Tropical cyclone: latent heat; eye warm with sinking air; eye-wall winds to 250 km/h; 600–1,200 km wide; recurve after 20°N; none in the South Atlantic/SE Pacific (cold seas).
- Naming: 6 RSMCs; WMO/ESCAP since 2000 — 8 + 5 (2018) = 13 countries; tornado over sea = waterspout.
keyPoints: Five air-mass types: mT, cT, mP, cP and cA (continental Arctic); front formation is frontogenesis.
Temperate cyclones form on the polar front; the faster cold front overtakes the warm front (occlusion) and the cyclone dissipates.
Tropical cyclones draw energy from latent heat of condensation; they die after landfall.
The eye is calm with subsiding, warmer air; not all cyclones develop an eye (UPSC 2020).
Eye-wall winds reach 250 km/h; Bay of Bengal storms are 600–1,200 km across and move 300–500 km a day.
Cyclones crossing 20°N usually recurve and are more destructive.
No tropical cyclones in the South Atlantic and south-east Pacific because sea-surface temperatures are low (UPSC 2015).
Six RSMCs worldwide; WMO/ESCAP naming since 2000 by 8 countries; 5 more joined in 2018 (Iran, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, UAE, Yemen).
Tornadoes occur mainly in middle latitudes; over the sea they are waterspouts.

items.title: Water in the Atmosphere — Humidity Measures, Evaporation & Fog vs Mist
items.body:
### Humidity, evaporation and condensation

**In one line**
Humidity is measured three ways — absolute, specific and relative; evaporation stores **latent heat** (about **600 calories per gram**), and condensation releases it as dew, frost, fog, mist or cloud.

**The story**
Water vapour matters because it sets the air's **potential for precipitation**, absorbs radiation (regulating heat loss), stores the **latent energy** that feeds storms, and even affects how fast our bodies cool.

| Measure | Definition | Unit |
|---|---|---|
| **Absolute humidity** | weight of water vapour in a unit volume of air | **grams per cubic metre** |
| **Specific humidity** | weight of water vapour per unit weight of air | **grams per kilogram** |
| **Relative humidity** | actual vapour ÷ capacity at that temperature | **percent**; higher over **oceans**, lower over continents |
| **Dew point** | temperature at which the air becomes **saturated** | °C |

**Evaporation** — turning about one gram of water into vapour takes about **600 calories**; this energy is released again on condensation, so it is called **latent heat**. Evaporation rises with **higher temperature**, **drier air** and **moving air** (wind replaces the saturated layer).

**Condensation** — depends on the **amount of cooling** and the **relative humidity**; air must cool **below the dew point**. Forms that appear **below freezing**: **frost**, snow, some clouds; **above freezing**: **dew**, **fog**, clouds.
- **Dew** — droplets on grass and leaves; needs a **clear sky, calm air, high relative humidity and cold, long nights**.
- **White frost** — ice crystals when the dew point is at or below 0°C.
- **Fog** — a cloud whose base is at or near the ground; urban smoke supplies nuclei, giving **smog**.
- **Mist** — contains **more moisture** than fog (each nucleus has a thicker water coat); common over **mountains** where rising warm air meets cold slopes. **Fogs are drier** and are common where **warm and cold currents meet**.

**PYQ (UPSC 2022)** — "High clouds mainly reflect sunlight and cool the surface" and "low clouds strongly absorb infrared and warm the surface" are **both wrong**: high thin clouds trap outgoing infrared (warming), low thick clouds reflect sunlight (cooling).

**Don't confuse**
Absolute = g per m³ (volume); specific = g per kg (mass). Mist is wetter than fog.

**TL;DR**
- Absolute (g/m³), specific (g/kg), relative (%) humidity; dew point = saturation temperature.
- About 600 calories evaporate 1 g of water — latent heat; evaporation rises with heat, dry air and wind.
- Dew above 0°C, frost below; dew needs clear, calm, humid, long nights.
- Mist wetter than fog; fog where warm and cold currents meet; smog = fog + smoke.
keyPoints: Absolute humidity is in grams per cubic metre; specific humidity in grams per kilogram; relative humidity in percent.
Relative humidity is greater over the oceans and lower over the continents.
About 600 calories convert one gram of water to vapour — latent heat.
Evaporation increases with temperature, dryness of air and air movement.
Condensation depends on the amount of cooling and relative humidity; air must cool below the dew point.
Dew needs a clear sky, calm air, high relative humidity and cold long nights.
Mist contains more moisture than fog and is frequent over mountains; fog is common where warm and cold currents meet.

items.title: Köppen Classification — Approaches, Letter Codes & Every Sub-type with Examples
items.body:
### Köppen's scheme in full

**In one line**
**Wladimir Köppen** (1918) built an **empirical** classification from temperature and rainfall values that match vegetation: five groups (A–E) plus highland **H**, each split by letter codes.

**The story**
Climates can be classified in three ways: **empirical** (on observed temperature and rainfall), **genetic** (on causes) and **applied** (for a purpose). Köppen's empirical scheme, linking climate to vegetation, is the most widely used. Of his five main groups, **four are temperature-based** (A, C, D, E) and **one** (**B**) is precipitation-based.

**What the letters mean**
- Second letter: **f** = no dry season, **m** = monsoon, **w** = dry winter, **s** = dry summer; for group B, **W** = desert, **S** = steppe; for group E, **T** = tundra, **F** = ice cap (frost).
- Third letter: **h** = hot (dry low latitude), **k** = cold (dry middle latitude), **a** = hot summer, **b** = warm summer.

| Group | Where | Sub-types and examples |
|---|---|---|
| **A** Tropical humid | between the tropics; Sun overhead, ITCZ | **Af** tropical wet — Amazon, western equatorial Africa; **Am** tropical monsoon — Indian subcontinent, northern Australia; **Aw** tropical wet-and-dry — Sudan, Brazil |
| **B** Dry | about 15°–60° N and S | **BSh** subtropical steppe; **BWh** subtropical desert — Sahara, Arabia; **BSk** mid-latitude steppe — Central Asia; **BWk** mid-latitude desert — **Great Basin** |
| **C** Warm temperate | about 30°–50° | **Cwa** humid subtropical with dry winter — **North Indian plains**, eastern China; **Cs** Mediterranean — California, Chile; **Cfa** humid subtropical, rain all year — eastern USA, southern China; **Cfb** marine west coast — north-western Europe, Pacific north-west |
| **D** Cold snow-forest | 40°–70°N (no southern equivalent) | **Df** humid winters — Canada, northern Russia; **Dw** dry winters — north-eastern Asia |
| **E** Polar | beyond 70° | **ET** tundra — permafrost, Arctic; **EF** ice cap — Greenland, Antarctica |
| **H** Highland | mountains | large changes over short distances |

**The India angle** — most of India is **Am** and **Aw**; the north Indian plains are **Cwa**; Rajasthan is **BWh/BSh**; Ladakh is a cold desert (**BWk**).

**Don't confuse**
Cs = dry **summer** (Mediterranean); Cw = dry **winter** (North India, China). BW = desert; BS = steppe.

**TL;DR**
- Köppen 1918, empirical, vegetation-based; A–E + H; B alone is precipitation-based.
- Af Amazon, Am India, Aw Sudan; BWh Sahara, BWk Great Basin, BSk Central Asia.
- Cwa North Indian plains, Cs California, Cfa eastern USA, Cfb NW Europe; Df Canada, Dw NE Asia.
- ET tundra (permafrost), EF ice cap (Greenland, Antarctica).
keyPoints: Three approaches to classification: empirical, genetic and applied; Köppen's (1918) is empirical.
Four Köppen groups are temperature-based; group B (dry) is precipitation-based.
f = no dry season, m = monsoon, w = dry winter, s = dry summer; W = desert, S = steppe; h = hot, k = cold.
Af Amazon basin; Am Indian subcontinent; Aw Sudan/Brazil.
BWh Sahara/Arabia; BSk Central Asia; BWk Great Basin.
Cwa North Indian plains and eastern China; Cs California and Chile; Cfa eastern USA; Cfb north-western Europe.
Df Canada and northern Russia; Dw north-eastern Asia; ET tundra (permafrost); EF ice cap (Greenland, Antarctica).

items.title: World Climatic Regions I — Equatorial, Savanna, Monsoon, Desert & Steppe
items.body:
**The story**

### Climatic regions of the tropics and dry lands

**In one line**
Moving away from the equator, the hot-wet **equatorial** climate gives way to the wet-and-dry **savanna**, the reversing-wind **monsoon**, the **hot deserts** of the trade-wind belt, and the temperate **steppe** grasslands of continental interiors.

**Equatorial (hot, wet)**
- Lies within about **5°–10°** of the equator (our source prints this as "50°N to 100°S" — a typo). Examples: Amazon, Congo, Malaysia, Indonesia (Java), Ecuador, Nigeria.
- Uniform heat, monthly means **24–27°C**, **no winter**, small daily and annual ranges; heavy, evenly spread rain (about **150–250 cm**, the source's "6 to 10 inches" is a misprint) with **two peaks near the equinoxes**.
- **Tropical rainforest** — the **Selvas** of the Amazon; hardwoods **mahogany, ebony, greenheart**; lianas and epiphytes; few single-species stands. Highlands such as the **Cameron Highlands** (Malaysia) are cooler.

**Savanna (Sudan type, tropical wet-and-dry)**
- Between the equatorial forests and the trade-wind deserts; most typical in **Sudan**; also Kenya, Nigeria, the **Brazilian Highlands**, northern Australia and India.
- Rain in summer (May–September in the north); over **80 cm** at Kano (Nigeria); temperatures 18–32°C; hottest just before the rains.
- Tall grass (up to 12 feet) with **acacia** and **baobab**; "parkland" or "bush-veld"; large herbivores and carnivores. The **Harmattan** brings dry Saharan dust.

**Tropical monsoon**
- About **5°–30°** N and S — India, Thailand, Indo-China, southern China, northern Australia.
- Seasonal wind reversal; annual rain about **200–250 cm**, over **1,000 cm** at **Mawsynram and Cherrapunji** (orographic); **over 70%** of rain in summer.
- Three seasons: hot dry (**March–June**), rainy (**mid-June–September**, the **burst**), cool dry (**October–February**, north-east winds, western disturbances).
- **Monsoon (deciduous) forests** — moist deciduous over **150 cm**, dry deciduous below; evergreen where rain exceeds 200–250 cm.

**Hot deserts**
- On the **western margins** of continents between **15° and 30°**, where **subtropical highs** (descending air), offshore **trade winds** and **cold currents** stop rain. Rain under **25 cm**.
- **Sahara** is the largest hot desert (about **3.5 million square miles**); others: Arabian, Kalahari, Thar, Great Australian, Mojave, Sonoran, **Atacama** (under 2 cm — the **driest place on Earth**). Libya recorded **57°C in 1922**. Daily range 14–25°C.
- Peoples: **Bushmen** (Kalahari), **Bindibu** and Aborigines (Australia) as hunter-gatherers; **Tuaregs** (Sahara), **Bedouins** (Arabia), Mongols (Gobi) as nomadic herders; diamond mines of the Kalahari, copper of Chile.

**Mid-latitude deserts** — continental interiors cut off by mountains: **Gobi**, Turkestan, **Patagonian**, and **Ladakh** in India; very cold winters.

**Steppe (temperate grassland)**
- Continental interiors in the westerly belt; rain **25–75 cm**; warm summers, cold winters, big annual range.

| Name | Region |
|---|---|
| Prairies | North America |
| Pampas | Argentina and Uruguay |
| Velds | South Africa |
| Pustaz (Puszta) | Hungary |
| Downs | Australia |
| Canterbury | New Zealand |
| Steppes | Eurasia (Chernozem soil of Ukraine) |

Grass is shorter than in the savanna and nearly treeless; the regions are the world's **granaries** and ranching lands.

**Don't confuse**
Selvas = equatorial forest (Amazon); Pampas = temperate grassland (Argentina). Savanna has scattered trees; steppe is almost treeless.

**TL;DR**
- Equatorial: 24–27°C, no winter, two equinoctial rain peaks, Selvas (mahogany, ebony).
- Savanna: Sudan type, summer rain, acacia/baobab, Harmattan.
- Monsoon: 5°–30°, 200–250 cm, Mawsynram >1,000 cm, three seasons, deciduous forests.
- Hot deserts on west margins 15°–30° (Sahara largest, Atacama driest); steppe names Prairies, Pampas, Velds, Puszta, Downs, Canterbury.
keyPoints: Equatorial climate: monthly means 24–27°C, no winter, two rainfall peaks near the equinoxes.
Equatorial rainforest of the Amazon is the Selvas — mahogany, ebony, greenheart.
Savanna (Sudan type) has summer rain; acacia and baobab trees; Kano (Nigeria) gets over 80 cm.
Tropical monsoon climate lies 5°–30°; over 70% of rain in summer; Mawsynram and Cherrapunji exceed 1,000 cm.
Hot deserts lie on the western margins of continents between 15° and 30°, with rain under 25 cm.
Sahara is the largest hot desert; Atacama (under 2 cm) is the driest; Libya recorded 57°C in 1922.
Bushmen (Kalahari), Tuaregs (Sahara), Bedouins (Arabia) are desert peoples.
Mid-latitude deserts: Gobi, Turkestan, Patagonian, Ladakh.
Temperate grasslands: Prairies (N. America), Pampas (Argentina), Velds (S. Africa), Puszta (Hungary), Downs (Australia), Canterbury (NZ).

items.title: World Climatic Regions II — Mediterranean, China, British, Taiga, Laurentian & Polar
items.body:
**The story**

### Climatic regions of the middle and high latitudes

**In one line**
West margins of the middle latitudes get the **Mediterranean** (30°–45°) and **British** types; east margins get the **China/Gulf/Natal** and **Laurentian** types; the continental north has the **Taiga**; and beyond the Arctic Circle lies the **Polar** climate.

**Mediterranean (warm temperate western margin)**
- **30°–45°** on the **western** sides of continents: the Mediterranean lands, **central Chile**, **California** (San Francisco), the **Cape Town** region, southern and south-western **Australia** (Adelaide, Perth).
- **Dry, warm summers** (offshore trade winds) and **wet, mild winters** (onshore **westerlies**, as the wind belts shift).
- Vegetation is **xerophytic**: evergreen oaks (**cork**), eucalyptus (Australia), giant **sequoia** (California), thorny shrubs; the region is famed for citrus fruit and grapes. Local winds: Sirocco, Mistral, Bora, Tramontana, Gregale.

**Warm temperate eastern margin** (about 20°–35°)

| Type | Where | Feature |
|---|---|---|
| **China type** | most of China | summer **south-east monsoon** from the Pacific; dry, cold **north-west monsoon** from the **Siberian high** in winter; typhoons |
| **Gulf type** | south-eastern USA | warm **Gulf Stream**; about **150 cm** rain; summer thunderstorms, **hurricanes** (Sept–Oct), **tornadoes** |
| **Natal type** | New South Wales, Natal, Parana–Paraguay–Uruguay basin | onshore trades all year; rain well spread; low range |
Rain 60–150 cm; eucalyptus in eastern Australia, **Parana pine, quebracho, yerba mate** in South America, palms in Natal.

**British type (cool temperate western margin)**
- **Britain** and north-west Europe (France, Belgium, Netherlands, Denmark, western Norway), coastal **British Columbia**; in the south, New Zealand's South Island, **Tasmania**, southern Chile.
- **Westerlies all year**, frequent **cyclones**; the warm **North Atlantic Drift** keeps winters mild; mean temperatures **5–15°C**; rain all year, decreasing eastward, autumn/winter maximum.
- **Deciduous forests** — oak, elm, ash, birch, beech, poplar; conifers on high ground.

**Taiga (cool temperate continental, Siberian, boreal — Köppen D)**
- **50°–70°N** from Canada across Scandinavia and Russia — **absent in the Southern Hemisphere** (no land at those latitudes).
- Winters **−30 to −40°C**, short cool summers, annual range **50–60°C**; **Verkhoyansk** in Siberia is among the coldest inhabited places; **Buran** and blizzards; precipitation only **38–63 cm**.
- **Evergreen coniferous forests** — pine, fir, spruce, **larch**; conical shape sheds snow, needle leaves cut transpiration; **podzol** soils (acidic, leached); prized **softwood** from pure stands — the base of **lumbering**.

**Laurentian (cool temperate eastern margin)**
- Only in the **Northern Hemisphere**: north-eastern North America (eastern Canada, north-east USA, Newfoundland) and eastern Asia (**North China, Manchuria, Korea, northern Japan**); in the south only eastern Patagonia, which is arid instead (rain shadow of the Andes).
- Cold dry winters, warm wet summers — about **two-thirds of rain in summer**; conifers north of 50°N, deciduous forests (oak, maple, beech) south of it.

**Polar (tundra and ice cap — Köppen E)**
- **Ice caps**: Greenland and **Antarctica** (the largest); **tundra**: Arctic coasts of Eurasia, northern Canada and Alaska.
- Warmest month **below 10°C**; only about four months above freezing; **permafrost**; growing season **under three months**; **no trees** — mosses, **lichens**, sedges, dwarf willows and birches; blizzards.

**Don't confuse**
Mediterranean = winter rain (west margin); China type = summer rain (east margin). Taiga = conifers (D); tundra = treeless (E).

**TL;DR**
- Mediterranean: 30°–45° west margins, dry summer, winter rain from westerlies, cork oak, sequoia, citrus.
- China type (SE monsoon summer, Siberian NW winter), Gulf type (hurricanes, tornadoes), Natal type.
- British type: westerlies, North Atlantic Drift, 5–15°C, deciduous forests.
- Taiga 50°–70°N only in the NH (Verkhoyansk, conifers, podzol); Laurentian NE America and NE Asia; Polar: <10°C, permafrost, mosses and lichens.
keyPoints: Mediterranean climate lies 30°–45° on west margins: central Chile, California, Cape Town, south and south-west Australia.
Mediterranean summers are dry (offshore trades); winters wet from onshore westerlies; cork oak, eucalyptus, sequoia.
China type: south-east monsoon in summer, dry north-west monsoon from the Siberian high in winter.
Gulf type (SE USA): Gulf Stream, ~150 cm rain, hurricanes and tornadoes; Natal type: rain well distributed.
British type: westerlies all year, North Atlantic Drift, mean 5–15°C, deciduous forests.
Taiga: 50°–70°N, absent in the Southern Hemisphere; annual range 50–60°C; Verkhoyansk; podzol soils; softwood lumbering.
Laurentian climate: NE North America and eastern Asia (Manchuria, Korea, N. Japan); two-thirds of rain in summer.
Polar climate: warmest month below 10°C; permafrost; growing season under three months; mosses, lichens and sedges.

items.title: Monsoon Mechanism in Detail — Jets, Tibet, Somali Jet, IOD & Western Disturbances
items.body:
### How the Indian monsoon works

**In one line**
The monsoon ("**mausim**" = season) depends not only on land–sea heating but on the **Tibetan Plateau**, the jump of the **subtropical westerly jet** north of the Himalayas, the **Tropical Easterly Jet**, the **Somali jet** and the **Indian Ocean Dipole**.

**The story**
Seasonal reversal of winds is the typical characteristic of the monsoon climate (UPSC 2014). The word **monsoon** comes from the Arabic **"mausim"** (season). It is a double system of seasonal winds — sea to land in summer, land to sea in winter — most pronounced over the Indian subcontinent. The **south-west monsoon** is driven by the intense **low over the Tibetan Plateau** and a permanent **high near Madagascar** in the southern Indian Ocean; the **north-east monsoon** by highs over Tibet and Siberia in winter.

**The jets**

| Feature | Key facts |
|---|---|
| Subtropical westerly jet (STJ) | in winter it is **split** by the Himalayas (physical barrier) and Tibet (thermal barrier); the **southern branch** blows south of the Himalayas along about **25°N** at about **240 km/h** (northern branch 70–90 km/h); the branches rejoin off **eastern China**; it blocks the monsoon from March to May |
| STJ shift | late May–June the STJ moves **north of the Himalayas/Tibet** — the trigger for the **sudden onset** (burst) |
| Tropical Easterly Jet (TEJ) | forms in early June **between 5° and 20°N**, about **6–9 km** up, blowing **east to west** across peninsular India to Africa; lasts till about October |
| Tibet snow | heavy, lasting **snow over Tibet** delays heating and the easterly jet → a **weak monsoon** |
| **Somali (Findlater) jet** | a low-level jet from Mauritius and Madagascar across the Kenya coast (about 3°S); speeds the monsoon towards India; its ocean current is the **Findlater current**, which causes **upwelling** off the Horn of Africa |

**Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD)**
- The SST difference between a **western pole in the Arabian Sea** (western Indian Ocean) and an **eastern pole south of Indonesia**.
- Develops **April–May**, **peaks in October**.
- **Positive IOD** — the western Indian Ocean is warmer, Indonesia cooler and drier — **good for the Indian monsoon**; negative IOD the reverse.
- Its atmospheric partner is **EQUINOO** (Equatorial Indian Ocean Oscillation).

**Withdrawal and winter**
Tibet cools from August–October, the STJ returns south of the Himalayas, the ITCZ moves south and dry, seaward winds set in. **Western disturbances** — cyclones from the **Mediterranean** carried east by the **westerly jet** — bring winter rain and snow to the north-west. The north-east monsoon gathers moisture over the **Bay of Bengal** and rains on the **Coromandel coast** (Tamil Nadu and south coastal AP), which is **dry in July–August**.

**Rainfall extremes and barriers**
- **Mawsynram and Cherrapunji** (Meghalaya) — over **1,100 cm** a year, from a **funnelling** effect plus orographic lift; **Jaisalmer** — rarely over **12 cm**.
- The **Himalayas** block cold Central Asian air (northern India is **3–8°C warmer** in winter than places at the same latitude) and stop the monsoon escaping into China.
- **Western Ghats** — heavy rain on the west, **rain shadow** over interior Maharashtra, Karnataka, Telangana, **Andhra Pradesh** (Rayalaseema) and Tamil Nadu.
- Monsoon winds run **parallel to the Aravallis**, so Rajasthan gets little rain (except Mount Abu).

**Don't confuse**
STJ = westerly, blocks the monsoon until it shifts north; TEJ = easterly, helps it. Somali jet (air) vs Findlater current (sea).

**TL;DR**
- "Mausim" = season; Tibet low + Madagascar high drive the SW monsoon.
- STJ split by the Himalayas (southern branch ~25°N, ~240 km/h); its June shift north triggers the burst; TEJ 5°–20°N, 6–9 km, E→W.
- Heavy Tibet snow → weak monsoon; Somali (Findlater) jet; Findlater current upwelling.
- IOD: Arabian Sea vs south of Indonesia, peaks October; positive IOD helps; EQUINOO; western disturbances from the Mediterranean.
keyPoints: "Monsoon" comes from the Arabic "mausim" (season).
SW monsoon is driven by the Tibetan low and the high near Madagascar.
Winter subtropical jet is split by the Himalayas and Tibet; the southern branch flows along ~25°N at ~240 km/h; branches rejoin off eastern China.
The northward shift of the STJ in late May–June triggers the sudden onset (burst) of the monsoon.
Tropical Easterly Jet: 5°–20°N, 6–9 km up, east to west, June to October.
Thick snow over Tibet → weak monsoon.
Somali (Findlater) jet aids the monsoon; the Findlater current causes upwelling off the Horn of Africa.
IOD = SST difference between the Arabian Sea and the eastern Indian Ocean south of Indonesia; develops April–May, peaks October; EQUINOO is its atmospheric part.
Western disturbances come from the Mediterranean, carried by the westerly jet.
Mawsynram/Cherrapunji exceed 1,100 cm (funnelling + orographic); Jaisalmer rarely gets 12 cm; Rayalaseema lies in the rain shadow of the Western Ghats.

items.title: For Mains — Atmosphere, Weather Hazards & Climate
items.body:
### For Mains — how this topic is framed in Paper-2

Mains (GS Paper-2 — clause **M2-15**, environmental geography: sustainable development, weather phenomena, natural hazards and disaster management; also **M2-11** physical geography of India & AP) treats this topic as **weather → hazard → people → policy**. Expect questions on the monsoon, cyclones, the heat budget/greenhouse effect, and disaster management with a strong AP coastal angle.

**Dimensions Mains asks (use as an answer skeleton)**

| Dimension | What to write |
|---|---|

**Facts, reports and schemes to quote**
- **Heat budget**: 100 units in = 35 reflected + 65 absorbed; enhanced greenhouse effect driven by CO₂/CH₄/N₂O.
- **IPCC AR6** on intensifying cyclones and erratic monsoons; the **Paris Agreement** (well below 2°C).
- **Disaster Management Act, 2005 → NDMA (PM-chaired), NDRF, NIDM, SDMA/APSDMA (CM-chaired), DDMA (Collector)**.
- **Sendai Framework (2015–2030)** — adopted in 2015 at Sendai, Japan; 4 priorities for action, 7 global targets; successor to the Hyogo Framework for Action.
- **AP cyclones**: Hudhud (2014, Visakhapatnam), Titli (2018), Michaung (2023), Montha (2025) — AP coast ~974 km.

**Who manages disasters in India**

| Body | Level | Chaired by / role |
|---|---|---|
| National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA) | national | constituted under the Disaster Management Act, 2005; chaired by the Prime Minister |
| National Disaster Response Force (NDRF) | national | the specialised force for on-ground response (under the Ministry of Home Affairs) |
| Andhra Pradesh State Disaster Management Authority (APSDMA) | state | chaired by the Chief Minister |
| District Disaster Management Authority (DDMA) | district | chaired by the Collector |

**The AP angle**
Andhra Pradesh depends on **both** monsoons — the SW monsoon for the Krishna–Godavari catchments and the **NE retreating monsoon (Oct–Dec)** for the coast and Rayalaseema — yet that same season brings **Bay-of-Bengal cyclones and storm surges** onto a low-lying deltaic coast. AP's **APSDMA Real-Time Governance** early-warning system and zero-casualty evacuation drives are quotable successes; mangrove shelter-belts (Coringa, Krishna) are an ecosystem-based defence.

**Use in answers**
- **Example to cite**: Cyclone Hudhud (2014) and the sharp fall in cyclone mortality after improved IMD warnings and evacuations.
- **Diagram idea**: a labelled tropical-cyclone cross-section (eye → eye wall → rain bands), or the SW/NE monsoon wind-reversal map.
- **Quote**: frame policy as a shift 'from relief-centric to prevention- and preparedness-centric' (DM Act 2005 / Sendai spirit).

- Answer mechanism → pattern → hazard → impact → governance → way forward, not a definitions list.
